config.title: Berlin Brutalist Architecture - FAQ
config.subtitle: Practical questions about seeing Berlin's concrete architecture without mislabelling every post-war building.

items.q: What is the best Brutalist building to see in Berlin?
items.a: Mäusebunker in Lichterfelde is the clearest specialist stop in this guide. Its sloping concrete body and projecting ventilation tubes make the building's former research purpose visible from outside. Plan it as an exterior visit rather than assuming public interior access.

items.q: Is St. Agnes in Berlin a Brutalist building?
items.a: St. Agnes is often discussed with Berlin Brutalism because of its heavy concrete form and its 1960s church design by Werner Düttmann. It is now used by König Galerie. Check the gallery's current information on the day if an interior visit matters to you.

It is better treated as an important post-war modernist residential building rather than a simple Brutalist label. Its repeated balconies and coloured loggias make a useful contrast with the more exposed, machine-like attitude of Mäusebunker.

items.q: Can I go inside Mäusebunker or Corbusierhaus?
items.a: Do not plan on it. Mäusebunker is best treated as an exterior stop, while Corbusierhaus is a residential building. View both from public space and respect entrances and residents rather than treating either one as a museum.

items.q: Where should I start a Berlin concrete architecture walk?
items.a: Start with St. Agnes if you are already spending time in Kreuzberg, or with Haus des Lehrers if Alexanderplatz is already on your route. Make Mäusebunker a separate detour when the building itself is the reason for the trip.
